source.title: Superposition Is Not Necessary: A Mechanistic Interpretability Analysis of Transformer Representations for Time Series Forecasting

page_placements.theme: Enlarging the dictionary adds dead, rare or low-sensitivity latents more than new concepts

record.tranche_reason: The study tests whether SAE dictionary expansion reveals functionally relevant superposed structure in PatchTST and reports little downstream effect. It does not directly test whether individual coarse features split into finer features.
record.gate_note: The paper measures forecasting degradation under SAE reconstructions, dead-latent rates, and forecast shifts under latent amplification. These are indirect tests of functional consequences, not measurements of feature correspondence, input partitions, or geometric directions. Granular table results are not all extracted below; see rows_left_out.
record.test_reason: The study trains ReLU/L1 SAEs at 0.5×, 1.0× and 4.0× dictionary sizes on single-layer PatchTST FFN activations, but only as a probe for superposition. It measures downstream MSE degradation, dead-latent rates, reconstruction MSE, L0 and forecast shifts under latent amplification. It never matches features across dictionary sizes, compares their directions, checks whether finer latents partition a coarser latent's inputs, or looks at hierarchy or absorption. Its measures are a related but different construct (functional relevance and utilization of the dictionary), so it does not test any version. It mentions splitting-like LLM results only in passing ('expanding the dictionary uncovers progressively more monosemantic features'). The record's 'tests/T5' with V1 marked tested is wrong.
record.authors_conclusion: The record's paraphrase is correct. The authors conclude that post-GELU FFN activations of single-layer PatchTST show no evidence of strong superposition, and that superposition is not necessary for competitive performance on standard forecasting benchmarks. They offer this as a mechanistic explanation for why linear models stay competitive.
record.recipe_differences: Trains ReLU SAEs with an L1 sparsity penalty on post-GELU FFN activations and sweeps dictionary size; evaluates reconstruction replacement, latent utilization, and forecast interventions rather than feature splitting or geometric correspondence.
record.method_sensitivity: Dead-latent rates differ substantially by benchmark: Traffic exceeds 60%, while most benchmarks are below 7%. The sparsity-calibration sweep shows L0 increases as the L1 penalty decreases, but the paper reports no corresponding downstream forecasting improvement.

fits_no_version.finding: SAE reconstruction replacement gave nearly flat forecasting degradation from 0.5× to 4.0× dictionaries (average difference 0.214%). Dead-latent rates in the 4.0× SAE reached 54.9–65.8% on Traffic (H≥192) and were ≤7% elsewhere.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: In single-layer PatchTST FFN activations, enlarging the SAE dictionary adds little functionally relevant structure.

fits_no_version.finding: Amplifying each of the top-10 latents of the 4.0× SAE by 5× shifted forecasts by about 0.031 MAE on average (max 0.061).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Forecasts of single-layer PatchTST are insensitive to amplification of dominant SAE latents.

fits_no_version.finding: Larger dictionaries give lower reconstruction MSE and higher L0 at every λ (Tables 2–3), without downstream forecasting gain.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Additional SAE latents improve reconstruction without improving downstream function in PatchTST.

record.problems: Only one task-specific transformer architecture is analyzed, at a single layer, and only post-GELU FFN activations are probed. The paper reports fixed random seeds and no uncertainty estimates for the results. Its functional measures do not directly examine feature splitting, feature matching, or input partitions.
record.rows_left_out: Tables 1 and 2 report separate dataset-by-horizon values for dictionary-scale degradation, dead latents, causal shifts, L0 sparsity, and reconstruction MSE; Table 3 reports sparsity-calibration values by dataset and penalty. These granular values are not extracted because the study's measures do not directly establish feature splitting, and the text-level summaries relevant to those measures are recorded above. Appendix B's zero-ablation results validate that the FFN is active but do not test the claim versions.

untested.parts: All: no cross-size feature matching, input coverage or direction comparison.
All: no large models or open SAE releases.
All: no feature families or hierarchy analysis.
All: no parent/child firing or absorption analysis.
All: no decomposition of larger-SAE latents into smaller-SAE latents, and no novel-latent analysis.
All: only an L1 λ sweep (L0 response); no alternative objectives such as Matryoshka SAEs, and no splitting measure.

record.verdict_notes: The reader's relation (tests/T5) and its V1 'tested' status should be dropped: none of its own rows bear on any version, and the study's measures (degradation, dead latents, intervention MAE) cannot show splitting. Table 2 (reconstruction MSE and L0 rising with size) also says nothing about feature correspondence. Small dictionaries (d_ff 32–256) and one seed per configuration.

versions.untested_parts: Tests scaling only through reconstruction effects and latent utilization; does not match small- and large-dictionary features, compare their directions, or test whether child features partition parent inputs.
No test of nested feature families, geometric closeness, or a concept hierarchy.
No parent-child firing or absorption analysis.
No decomposition of larger-SAE latents into smaller-SAE latents, or test for novel latents and canonical units.
The study calibrates the L1 sparsity penalty but does not measure splitting under different objectives or test Matryoshka SAEs.

relation.reason: The study never tests feature splitting. It mentions the LLM dictionary-scaling finding ('expanding the dictionary uncovers progressively more monosemantic features') only as background for a superposition probe.

tranche.reason: The study uses SAEs only to probe superposition in single-layer PatchTST FFN activations. It never compares latents across dictionary sizes or checks whether features split, so T5 does not fit.

source_check.notes: This study tests superposition in a time-series transformer, not feature splitting, and the word 'split' never appears. It reports downstream MSE degradation, dead latents, L0 and reconstruction MSE across 0.5x/1.0x/4.0x SAEs, but no comparison of latents across sizes. The 0.214% figure is a mean absolute gap in percentage points of degradation.

statements.problem: None. 0.214% is the text's average 0.5x vs 4.0x difference, and it reproduces from Table 1 as the mean absolute gap over 32 cells. Traffic dead latents are 54.9/65.8/63.5% at H=192/336/720. Every other cell, Traffic H=96 included, is 0.0-7.0%, the maximum being Exchange H=96 at 7.0%. 'Nearly flat' matches the text.
